content: An excoriation refers to the erosion or destruction of the skin caused by mechanical means, such as scratching or abrasion. It often presents as a visible scratch or superficial damage to the skin. This condition is frequently observed in association with other skin disorders that cause itching or pruritus, such as dry skin, dermatitis, atopic dermatitis, and scabies. Excoriations can also occur as a symptom of systemic illnesses, such as liver failure, where pruritus is triggered by elevated levels of bilirubin in the body. The term excoriation can also be linked to neurotic excoriations, which are considered to have a psychiatric origin. Patients with neurotic excoriations are advised to avoid picking or scratching their skin. If lesions are found in areas of the body that are not easily accessible to the hands, an alternative diagnosis should be considered, as this reduces the likelihood of neurotic excoriations, though it does not entirely rule it out. This condition is more commonly observed in females than in males. The most frequently affected areas include the face, neck, back, and extremities. The damage to the skin is typically caused by behaviors such as rubbing, scratching, or picking. Severe itching from other underlying causes may mimic the appearance of this disorder, making diagnosis challenging. Diagnosis is often made by exclusion, meaning other potential causes are ruled out. One diagnostic approach involves bandaging the affected areas to prevent further scratching. If the lesions improve or there is a noticeable change in the patient’s behavior, this supports the diagnosis of neurotic excoriations. Treatment options may include periodic bandaging of the affected areas, psychiatric counseling to address underlying psychological factors, and lifestyle adjustments. Topical treatments, such as lotions with or without menthol and phenol, may be used to provide relief and reduce the urge to scratch. In some cases, antidepressant medications may be effective for patients with neurotic excoriations. Other medications, such as antihistamines taken at bedtime, antipruritic agents, pimozide, or topical corticosteroids, may be prescribed if the scratching is due to another underlying condition. However, these treatments are typically reserved for other diagnoses, and further evaluation should be conducted to determine the root cause of the symptoms.
